en: Compiled by Shi Dunlun from the *Lunben* (Treatise Texts), Volume Twenty, Part One, Section Twelve:

The Stage of That Accomplished through Cultivation (*bhāvanā-mayī-bhūmi*). "Accomplished through cultivation" (*bhāvanā-mayī*) means "cultivation" (*bhāvanā*). This refers to the cultivation that gives rise to wisdom through superior meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
Because it serves as an antidote, the wisdom that understands both principle and phenomena, which is produced by concentration, is called "cultivated wisdom" (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*). This wisdom,
along with its associated mental states and mental factors, as well as the fruits obtained— whether conditioned or unconditioned— all constitute the essence of this stage.
The main text is divided into two parts:
first, concluding the preceding section and introducing the subsequent inquiry;
second, providing the formal explanation in response to that inquiry.
The commentary consists of three parts:
first, the listing of the four bases;
second, a detailed explanation through the mutual inclusion of the seven branches.
In the subsequent summary that establishes the stage of that which is cultivated through meditation (*bhāvanā-mayī-bhūmi*),
within the detailed explanation of the inclusion of the seven branches,
the first part provides a general enumeration of the inclusion of these seven branches.
The characteristics will be analyzed in detail later.
The initial passage consists of three parts;
first is the heading.
Next is the enumeration;
finally is the conclusion.
"Place" refers to the location.
Because cultivation is perfected only by relying on the four bases of meaning:
first, the internal essence and external conditions within the locus must both be complete;
second, the causal conditions for practicing the mundane and supramundane methods of cultivation.
Third is the cultivation of yoga, which is the actual essence of correct cultivation.
Fourth is the cultivation of the fruit, which refers to the fruits of mundane and supramundane conditioned and unconditioned merits obtained through the preceding cultivation.
Regarding the summary of the seven branches:
first, the perfection of birth is the basis for cultivation;
second, the perfection of hearing the true Dharma; third, taking nirvāṇa as the foremost; and fourth, the accomplishment of the wisdom that brings liberation to maturity.
These three aforementioned types are called the cultivation of causes and conditions.
Fifth, the cultivation of antidotes is called the cultivation of yoga.
Sixth is mundane purity.
The seven supramundane purities are the fruits of cultivation.
Among the detailed distinctions of the characteristics of the seven branches,
they are subsumed under four points.
It is divided into four parts.
Within the first section, "The Place for Cultivating the Perfection of Initial Birth," the text consists of three parts.
First, the perfection of birth is analyzed;
next, the yoga practice that subsumes the four branches is presented;
finally, the perfection of birth is concluded by summarizing the meaning of the extensive holy teachings, neither adding nor subtracting.
The initial section further consists of three parts:
first, the question that sets forth ten types;
second, the individual exposition of each.
This concludes the summary.
Furthermore, regarding the statement "being born in a central land and not in a frontier region," Master Tai said:
Only Central India (Madhyadeśa) is called the Middle Kingdom;
although the other four regions of India have the fourfold assembly traveling and coming and going there, they are all termed "borderlands" (pratyantajanapada).
There is no correct phonetic transcription for the name Dāxū that can be translated.
Although "shibie" (discrimination) carries the meaning of being perverse and rebellious,
"Miecilieche" (Mleccha) likewise has no phonetic equivalent that can be translated [into Chinese].
"Wusuo shibie" (lack of discrimination) carries the meaning of being dull-witted and ignorant.
In these latter two locations, there are no wandering assemblies of the fourfold community,
nor do noble ones dwell therein.
Since there is a distinction between the conscious and the unconscious, they are divided into four places.
First, Central India is so named because the Buddhas of the three periods of time are born therein.
Second, although the four regions of India have no Buddhas appearing there, the fourfold assembly travels there to provide instruction and guidance.

In three or four Indic countries, during the time when the Buddha was in the world, although there were no members of the fourfold assembly wandering abroad, there were those capable of discernment; for example, the country known as Daśapura (達須國) is like the country of Tang (唐國).
The four groups—the Yi, Di, Rong, and Qiang—are called Mleccha.
Jingji explains this in the same way as the Śramaṇas;
it is according to what is commonly said in the secular traditions of the Western Regions.
Only the five regions of India are called the Middle Kingdom;
all others are considered borderlands.
Regarding the transmission of the Buddha-dharma, only Central India is designated as the Middle Kingdom.
The rest are called the borderlands.
Duke Jing further said:
"As for the Mlecchas..."
They are called the defiled and impure;
the Turks and others are of such lowly and base classes.
This refers precisely to the various kingdoms located east of the Pamir Mountains (Congling).
Master Ji stated:
"Dāsu refers to those who are fragmented, base, evil, vulgar, and lowly."
The Mlecchas delight in filth and impurity.
According to the *Carmavastu* (Chapter on Leather) of the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*,
Mahākātyāyana was residing in the country of Aparāntaka.
He sent Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa to inquire after the World-Honored One’s health on Vulture Peak Mountain and to request five matters;
among these,
one was the request that those from border regions be permitted to receive the precepts in groups of five.
The Buddha permitted that in the country of Avanti, five persons who uphold the Vinaya may receive the full ordination (*upasampadā*).
He also permitted this for other regions.
As for "other regions," there is a country in the east named Pāṭaliputra.
Outside [the monastery], one may listen.
To the south there is a stūpa named Jingshan (Peaceful Virtue).
Outside that stūpa, one may listen.
In the west there is a country with a mountain named Ekaśṛṅga, the Mountain of the Rishi Lineage;
outside [the city], he then listened.
In the north there is a country named Stambha.
Regarding the *Bai-shui-tiao* (White Water Tune) performed outside the palace precincts,
Vinaya Master Xuán states:
During the Liang dynasty, he came from the northwest to pay court at the Liang capital.
According to the relevant Vinaya texts,
"the Middle Kingdom" appears to refer broadly to many regions rather than being restricted solely to Central India.
Below "Hearing the perfect True Dharma," the second [section],
the explanation of the causes and conditions for cultivation,
is divided into three parts.
First, the three branches are explained in detail.
Next, following the sequence already established for the three branches, the conclusion is made that the extensive teaching neither exceeds nor lacks anything.

Finally, it is concluded that these three branches should be understood as the causal conditions for practicing yoga, thereby establishing that they are subsumed within the causal conditions for cultivation.

Furthermore, the correct teaching of the Dharma is briefly of two kinds, namely: that which is conformable and that which is undefiled. As will be explained at length in twenty sections in the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*, this correct teaching of the Dharma conforms to the true suchness (*tathatā*) revealed by the two kinds of emptiness.
Furthermore, because one teaches others without expectation,
there is no defilement.
Within that which has Nirvana as its foremost, [this is so].
The broad meaning is presented in three parts: first the question, next the explanation, and finally the conclusion.
Within the explanation, there are two sections:
first, the explanation of nirvāṇa as the supreme characteristic; second, the explanation of how, by means of this, one attains five benefits.
The initial section further consists of two parts.
First, it generally clarifies that taking *nirvāṇa* as the primary objective, one listens to the true Dharma without being distracted by other conditions.
Second, it explains "taking as the primary objective" through ten successive turns.
The latter section has two parts:
first, the presentation of the ten turnings;
second, the subsequent explanation of the ten turnings, beginning with Nirvana.
Regarding the "ten turnings":
first, taking the wisdom derived from hearing as the cause;

second, giving rise to three kinds of faith toward the path and its fruit—first, faith in the reality of the truths; next, faith in the reality of the precepts; and finally, faith in one's own capability.
As stated in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*:
third, distancing oneself from clamor and all evil discursive thoughts;
fourth, proceeding toward the wisdom consisting of reflection that is well-determined regarding the wholesome.
Fifth, the ability to enter into the two methods of cultivation;
sixth, the realization of the wisdom of cultivation;
seventh, the arousal of aspiration for nirvana and aversion toward saṃsāra.
The eighth is the liberation of the learner (*śaikṣa*) through the clear realization of the truths (*satyābhisamaya*).
The ninth is the liberation of the non-learner (*aśaikṣa*) through the repeated cultivation of the path.
The first five occur prior to the applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), the meditation on impurity (*aśubhabhāvanā*), and so forth.
The next one abides in the stage of the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-saṃjñā*) and so forth;

the next one abides in the four roots of goodness (*catvāri kuśalamūlāni*), because it gives rise to longing for nirvāṇa and aversion toward saṃsāra; thus, the latter two [roots] may be understood as following the contemplation of the Four Truths (*catur-āryasatya*).
These nine aforementioned [factors],
with nirvana without remainder as their foremost, lead to the realization of the nirvana without remainder;
this constitutes the tenth.
Furthermore, when these nine types of *sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* (nirvāṇa with remainder) are taken as the foremost, it is called the "fulfillment of liberation.
This very liberation, moreover, takes *anupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* (nirvāṇa without remainder) as its foremost.
Regarding the five benefits:
there are two advantages when hearing the true Dharma,
and likewise two advantages when practicing correct conduct.
And one realizes the limit of suffering.
Regarding the maturation of the wisdom that brings liberation to fruition, there are two parts:
first the question, and then the answer.
The answer consists of three parts:
first, it clarifies that śamatha and vipaśyanā are matured by means of wisdom;

second, it clarifies that associating with virtuous friends and practicing the three trainings are matured by means of wisdom; and finally, it clarifies the ten methods for maturing the wisdom that brings liberation to maturity.
Liberation refers to the fruit;
that which can ripen it refers to the cause, namely,
calm abiding (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*), and so forth.
Both this fruit and this cause are that which is ripened;
wisdom is that which ripens. Because it is able to ripen them, [wisdom is called "ripening"].
This is called the maturation of wisdom.
Regarding the phrase "because wisdom within a concentrated mind operates with purity toward the objects of knowledge," this explains the perfection of wisdom through the branch of *śamatha*.
If the concentrated mind lacks wisdom, the object of realization will not be clear and defilements will not be abandoned.
It is through the clarity of wisdom that one is able to abandon obstacles; thus, the concentrated mind becomes perfected, which is called the accomplishment of wisdom.
Second, following the section on the factors of *vipaśyanā*,
the text explains how one trains in the three learnings by relying on a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) through the maturation of wisdom;
this consists of an initial statement followed by an explanation.
In the summary:
first, the arising of cultivated wisdom (bhāvanāmayī-prajñā) necessarily depends on being sustained by a virtuous friend;
second, it depends on being sustained by śamatha.
Third, it is encompassed by the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla*).
Because the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*) has not yet initially arisen, it is not said to be encompassed by the wisdom of cultivation;
alternatively, because the wisdom of hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*) has not yet initially arisen, it is not said to be encompassed by [simply] "wisdom."
Because the wisdom of skillful means has not yet been put into practice,
even the wisdom that arises subsequently is logically subsumed by that [prior] wisdom.
This will be explained further in the subsequent detailed exposition.
This explains only that [the mind] is sustained by a virtuous friend and by ethical discipline (*śīla*), but does not explain its being sustained by meditative concentration (*samādhi*);
for the previously accomplished calm abiding (*śamatha*) is precisely this [sustenance].
Regarding being sustained by a virtuous friend:
because one is sustained by a virtuous friend when the Dharma is being taught,
one possesses wisdom and possesses clear comprehension regarding the objects of knowledge within that taught Dharma.
Regarding "embraced by ethical discipline" (śīla):
because one is embraced by ethical discipline,
others may apply the three bases [of censure], such as the formal accusation of an offense.
Because of possessing wisdom, one is able to endure criticism and debate.
Thirdly, based on the reality of the objects of knowledge (*jñeya-tattva*), the following explains the ten methods for maturing the wisdom that ripens liberation.
There are two parts:
first, the analysis of the ten types;
second, the conclusion that these ten types can, through their gradual progression, bring liberation to full perfection.
Regarding the ten kinds:
first, the desire for true awareness and understanding regarding objects;
second, the delight in hearing the Dharma.
Third, he immediately poses questions for clarification;
fourth, he hears profound meanings of the Dharma never heard before;
fifth, through the illumination of the pure meaning of the Dharma, he eliminates his previous doubts.
Sixth, they are able to perceive faults and defects, and thus feel profound revulsion toward worldly success.
Seventh, they do not give rise to longing or desire for worldly prosperity.
Eighth, they generate right aspirations with the aim of eliminating the factors that lead to rebirth in the miserable realms.
Ninth, one cultivates all wholesome dharmas in order to eliminate all afflictions.
Tenth, one generates the correct aspiration with a mind seeking purity in order to attain those fruits;
through this gradual process, liberation becomes perfected.
Regarding the conclusion that these three branches comprehensively encompass the sacred teachings without any further additions:
as for the statement that "the meaning of these three branches of the extensive sacred teachings consists of ten sets of ten," Jing says:
Previously, within the fourth section, ten factors were analyzed as those which bring about the perfection of wisdom;
because wisdom is perfected, liberation is perfected.
Now, in this subsequent section, the perfection is elucidated by comprehensively integrating the mutually establishing characteristics of the preceding alternative formulations.
That is to say, by virtue of the second limb among the seven—the perfection of hearing the Dharma—one attains the third, the preeminence of nirvāṇa;
and by virtue of the preeminence of nirvāṇa, one attains the fourth, the maturation of the wisdom that ripens liberation.
Thus, within each of these three branches of the Buddha’s holy teaching, there are ten broad categories of analysis.
Therefore, it is said that the meaning of these three branches of the extensive holy teaching consists of ten sets of ten.
Thus, each of the three branches has ten modes of analytical exposition, making "ten tens. Ji states:
This means that because one first hears the True Dharma, whatever practice one performs takes *nirvāṇa* as its primary objective.
All these trainings that can bring about those stages such as liberation are the accomplishment of wisdom.
Following these two types, there are ten dharmas that proceed, preceded by hearing the two kinds of teachings and having nirvāṇa as their primary focus.
Within the accomplishment of wisdom, there are ten kinds of gradual stages;
therefore, the extensive teaching is summarized as "ten tens.
This does not mean that there are also ten [stages] for hearing the true Dharma.
Therefore, it is heard that within the True Dharma there is no extensive teaching regarding fetters (saṃyojana) that exceeds or adds to [the standard].
In the latter two [realms], there are fetters.
Among the seven branches:
The fifth is the cultivation of the remedies, which is the third cultivation of yoga among the four points.
The text is divided into four parts;
first is the general introduction by way of a question.
Next, the specific explanations follow:
third, cultivating the remedies is itself the cultivation of yoga;
fourth, the summary concludes that the extensive teachings do not exceed nor add anything to this.
Within the detailed explanation, there are three parts.
First, the explanation of the ten types of cultivation in the three stages.
Second, furthermore, regarding the perception of impurity (*aśubha-saṃjñā*), there are briefly two kinds; this follows the previous difficulty and provides an explanation.

Third, regarding those who cultivate various perceptions through right application (*samyak-prayoga*), they are able to sever and extinguish the various desires that are to be countered; this explains the extensive cultivation of the remedies (*pratipakṣa*).
The initial section has two parts.
First, three positions are listed;
subsequently, the ten cultivations are explained.
Within the explanation of the ten cultivations, there are three sections.
First, the two perceptions of impurity and impermanence are clarified.
Second, from "Furthermore, for one who has gone forth, there are four things to be done," the four perceptions of impermanence, suffering, and so forth are clarified.
Third, from "Furthermore, regarding dwelling in seclusion and solitude," the four perceptions of light and so forth are clarified.
Regarding the ten types of what is to be counteracted,
Jing says: "Within the stage of the householder, there are two."
First, one cultivates the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*) as an antidote for attachment arising toward one's wife.
Second, one cultivates the contemplation of impermanence (*anitya-bhāvanā*) as an antidote for affection arising toward other relatives and various material possessions.
Within the stage of renunciation (*pravrajyā-avasthā*), there are four [contemplations].
There are also four in the state of detachment;
thus, there are ten types in total.
Baso (Kuiji) says:
First, householders possess sensual desire and craving for enjoyments.
Second, those who have gone forth are disturbed by discursive thoughts and do not give rise to joy;
therefore, to eliminate sensual greed, they cultivate the perception of impurity (*aśubha-saṃjñā*).
One cultivates the perception of impermanence (*anityasaṃjñā*) in order to eliminate craving for enjoyments and to prevent the arising of delight.
This demonstrates that the cultivation of the perception of impermanence applies to both the lay and monastic stages;
by means of these two [capacities], one eliminates the two objects to be eliminated.
Therefore, it is said that they follow the sequence;
it is not that being a householder and being a renunciant constitute two names following the sequence.
Among the four perceptions—of impermanence, suffering, and so forth—there are three.
First, the four kinds of activities are explained;
next, the four kinds of objects to be remedied are explained;
finally, the four kinds of remedial methods are explained.
Below this are the remaining eight factors, consisting of the objects to be remedied and their respective remedies.
Specifically, after having gone forth, if one experiences joy and pleasure yet still gives rise to indolence, laziness, and so forth, these constitute four [factors].
Furthermore, while dwelling in seclusion and solitude, if there is mental obscurity regarding the categories of tranquility (śamatha) and insight (vipaśyanā), these constitute another four.
Therefore, regarding the life of renunciation, four types of obstacles arise with respect to the four kinds of tasks to be performed.
To eliminate these, one cultivates the four perceptions such as impermanence.
Among the four perceptions such as light, there are two [that are included here].
First, the four types of counteracted factors are explained;
subsequently, the four perceptions are explained.

Regarding the statement that "the mind possesses a characteristic of movement following along with birth-existence (*upapattibhava*), and as an antidote to this, one cultivates the perception of cessation (*nirodhasaṃjñā*"): [this means that] because the mind follows along with the characteristics of movement within birth-existence, one cultivates the perception of cessation as its antidote.
All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) arise, perish, and fluctuate; this is called the "perception of arising and movement.
Now, seeing that perception, it is termed the "perception of following movement within arising.
To counteract this, one cultivates the characteristic of cessation (*nirodhalakṣaṇa*), which is free from such shifting and movement.
Alternatively, there may arise in the future a sense of delight regarding repeated births, which is called the perception of movement (*anuvicarita-saṃjñā*).
To counteract this, one should cultivate the sign of cessation (*nirodha-nimitta*),
maintaining a state of non-arising and a mind free from longing for existence.
Although there are these two interpretations,
the former explanation is superior.
Furthermore, regarding the passage "impurity-perception is briefly of two kinds," [it continues as follows:]
The second section, which addresses and resolves the preceding objections, is divided into three parts:
first, an explanation of the initial characteristic of impurity for those living as householders;
second, an explanation of the cultivation of the perception of suffering regarding impermanence by those who have gone forth.
Third, regarding the three explanations of cultivating the perception of light and the perception of impurity while dwelling in seclusion,
there are three parts within this section.
First, two powers are enumerated;
next, the two obstacles are clarified;
and finally, it is explained that the remedial dharmas which eliminate these obstacles have many functions.
"Discernment" refers to correct reflection;
"cultivation" refers to the arising of practice.
Regarding the explanation of obstacles:
First, the obstacles are analyzed;
finally, they are summarized.
Among the five obstacles:
One who frequents the vicinity of women is frequently drawn near to them;
one who dwells in public places loses mindfulness.
That is to say, when encountering superior and manifest objects before a multitude,
those who remain in seclusion and are heedless indulge in unrestrained and perverse thoughts while dwelling alone in private.
Regarding the phrase "the appearance or disappearance of the object of focus depends on the power of habitual practice":
due to this habitual practice, the object may become obscured or manifest;

through loss of mindfulness and heedlessness, even when one exerts effort and so forth while cultivating the meditation on impurity, wrong thoughts and superior mental states may follow along with notions of purity.
Regarding the seven kinds of hindrances:
first, the nature of mental distraction regarding one's fundamental duties.
Jing says:
The fundamental cause of distraction is the desire for sensual pleasure. Xie says:
when one recollects the actions performed in the past, the mind immediately becomes distracted.
This refers to the impairment of wisdom through cultivation. Jì (基) says:
"When performing those activities, the mind becomes distracted."
Regarding the statement that "the two perform the activity of functioning toward their objects," Jing says:
"The expedient means of dispersing [the mind] is greed."
Tài said: "Recalling one's past deeds, their tendencies, and their formations also obstructs the cultivation of wisdom."
Baso says: "The 'skillfulness in the three types of preparatory attention' refers to the functional activity that initiates the inclination toward and engagement with those [specific] tasks."
Jingyun said:
"Nowadays, children have greedy hearts and desire to take the food and drink of the Buddhas and the Sangha;
they do not understand how to show respect, nor do they diligently inquire of their teachers about what is transgression and what is not."
Jizang said:
"Just as one who lacks wisdom uses the property of the Triple Gem,
because they do not respectfully serve their teachers and friends nor diligently inquire [of them], they do not understand the skillful means."
Fourth, although dwelling in a secluded place,
one fails to guard the sense-faculties and remains distracted by defiled discursive thoughts.
Fifth, one lacks moderation regarding food, such that the body is not well-adjusted.
Sixth, due to the disturbance of discursive investigation,
one does not delight in tranquil stillness.
Because the seven bodies are not disciplined,
one does not cultivate the category of wisdom that observes all phenomena.
It should be understood that all such counteractive factors are collectively explained as twelve in one section and fourteen in another.
Jingji likewise says:
"In discussing the two distinct obstacles,
there are five in the former and seven in the latter."
These are called the twelve;
when the general and specific categories are combined, two further general categories are added, namely:
the obstacles to analytical investigation and the obstacles to cultivation.
Thus, they total fourteen. Tai states:
"These are [the factors] from among the latter seven dharmas: lack of respect, requesting, the sense-gates, and disturbance."
If taken collectively as one, there are only seven factors;
if divided into two and including the defiled vitarka as a third,
there are thus fourteen.
In the explanation of the perception of light, there are three parts.
First, a general clarification of this light that takes phenomena as its object.
Second, a clarification of the eleven types of darkness and obstructions to be remedied.
"Third, it reveals the white dharmas that act as antidotes to what is contrary [to them].
Regarding the phrase 'because such doubt persists,' this concludes the first obscuration of darkness."
Regarding the phrase "because they can dispel the causes and conditions for obstacles and doubt":
this summarizes the final three types of obstacles—
diligence, little sleep, proper diet, physical harmony, and the correct contemplation of the truths of the Dharma.
Not desiring to dwell among the mixed [laity] and applying attention in accordance with reality are the causes and conditions that can eliminate doubt;
these pertain to the latter three obstacles.
Therefore, it is said that they are obstacles which can dispel doubt.
Regarding the seven types of darkness removed by the wisdom produced through cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*):
the first is torpor (*styāna*).
Second, restlessness;
third, joy; fourth, the two types of factors associated with fear and anger, and so forth.
Fifth, the arising of speech, vitarka, and vicāra;
sixth, improper mental attention and mental distraction;
seventh, wrong conceptualization.
Following that sequence, the seventh type of obscuration of darkness removed by the wisdom of cultivation is explained below,
under the heading "Purity in all aspects regarding the mundane.
This explains the fourth fruit of cultivation.
The text is divided into two parts:
first, the explanation of the two purities;
second, the conclusion establishing the fruit of cultivation.
This section is further divided into two parts:
first, the explanation of the sixth factor, the worldly purification;
second, the explanation of the seventh factor, the supramundane purification.
The initial section further has two parts:
first, an extensive explanation of the characteristics;
second, a conclusion that worldly purity exists only within the True Dharma and not among the various non-Buddhist paths.
The initial text has three parts:
first, the question enumerating the three names;
second, the detailed explanation of each.
The extensive teaching on the three fetters does not exceed nor add to this.
Regarding the specific explanation of these three:
first attaining the preliminary concentration (*anāgamya*) of the first dhyāna is termed "attaining samādhi."
Attaining the stage of the fundamental [dhyāna] is called the perfection of samādhi.
Being free from all obstructive defilements and giving rise to distinct supernormal knowledges that are pure and pristine white is called mastery over samādhi.
The attainment of samādhi is divided into four parts.
First, the specific characteristics of the objects to be abandoned and their antidotes are explained;
next, the meaning of "attainment" is explained as the attainment of the preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*).
The three summaries of the extensive teaching neither exceed nor add to it;
the four summaries are attained by those who dwell in the pure, mundane True Dharma.
The first section has two parts.
First, the twenty factors to be remedied are clarified;
second, the remedies that counteract them are revealed.
The first section further consists of two parts.
First, the twenty obstacles are explained;
subsequently, the four characteristics of the obstructive factors regarding capability are explained.
The first section consists of three parts.
First the heading, second the explanation, and finally the conclusion.
Within the perfection of *samādhi*, there are three parts;
first, the explanation of the ten characteristics.
Next, one binds the perfection and enters the fundamental stage.
Afterwards, one binds the extensive teaching.
As for the ten characteristics:
First, fulfilling the supreme meditative concentration of aspiration;
second, possessing the supreme virtues of concentration;
third, diligent and energetic exertion.
Fourth, subduing attachment to form;
fifth, being superior even to those who have not yet perfected their cultivation because they excel at overcoming the evils of others;
sixth, having a mind free from attachment when reborn among the gods of the Pure Abodes.
7. Not disparaging oneself; 8. Increasing cultivation; 9.
Cultivating in accordance with the two [types of] cultivation;
10. Exhorting and requesting the True Dharma.
Tenth, there is the arising of affection and delight toward śamatha and vipaśyanā.
Regarding mastery over samādhi, there are two parts;
first is the explanation of the characteristics of that mastery.
The subsequent section concludes the extensive teaching.
The initial text has three parts.
First, it indicates that although [the practitioner] has already attained perfection, because they have not yet mastered the characteristics of thorough observation, they shall attain mastery.
Next, the twenty-two aspects of the four stations (*catvāri sthānāni*) are explained.
Following that, under the section "He [attains mastery] in these four stations," the aspect of mastery (*vaśitva-lakṣaṇa*) is clarified.
Within this second passage, there are two parts.
First, four locations are listed;
subsequently, from the passage beginning with "having shaved off the hair and beard," twenty-two types of characteristics are explained.
As for these four locations:
First, the vow to personally undertake inferior physical appearance, deportment, and requisites;
second, the vow to personally undertake the restraint of the śīla;
third, the vow to personally undertake the diligent cultivation of wholesome dharmas.
Fourth, in order to abandon all suffering, when practicing the first three stages, one should correctly observe that various sufferings follow along.
Within these four stages, the first three each give rise to five aspects.
The seventh aspect arises from the fourth stage.
Regarding the five aspects of the first stage:
the first is the shaving off of hair and beard.
Second, abandoning the physical excellence of worldly appearance;
third, wearing robes of discolored hue.
These three marks arise from the undertaking of vows to assume an inferior form.
Furthermore, the various requisites of deportment each constitute one [of the five], making five.
Regarding the five characteristics of the second location, Tai says:
Taken together, these five characteristics do not exceed two types.
First, abandoning two matters immediately upon initial renunciation constitutes two characteristics.
Second, regarding the subsequent practice, there are three characteristics: first, being without violation of the precepts.
Second, because one is personally free from transgressions, one is able to properly point out the offenses of others.
Third, regarding any deficiencies in the precepts, one is able to repent once they have been committed.
Jing and Ji provide a similar interpretation.
First, it is manifested by the brief relinquishing of two matters.
Second, one does not reproach oneself nor is one censured and expelled by others.

Nanda and others do not accept the doctrine that seeds exist inherently; they explain this passage as follows:
"Just as a woman who can give birth is said to possess the seed of a person."
However, a female body has never contained a fetus;
this case is likewise, for it is capable of attaining realization, and thus it is said that there is a "seed.
This sense of capability is not something acquired through cultivation.
Therefore, this is the natural order.
Within the second section on the "Establishment of the Gates," there is first the heading,
followed by the explanation, and finally the conclusion.
The explanation consists of four parts:
first, clarifying the coarse and the subtle;
second, clarifying the continuity of the one and the many.
Regarding the third point, whether one encounters conditions for parinirvāṇa; and regarding the fourth point, the superior or inferior nature of those conditions—
one should answer that they are subtle and so forth.
Jingyun: When the lineage has not yet produced the fruit,
it has not yet cultivated the fruition.
Because its function has not yet increased and it remains subtle and hidden, it is called "subtle";
it is merely termed the "nature-lineage" (prakṛti-gotra).
Later, if it increases by virtue of conditions,
when it has already given its fruit,
it has already become a fully cultivated result.
Whether it be the seed or the fruit,
both are said to be coarse;
although this is an old seed, [it is still so designated].
That which has increased and departed is called the "cultivated seed" (*śrutavāsanā-bīja*).
Newly perfumed seeds are also called the "cultivated seed.
Here, the meaning of the "stage of the spiritual lineage" (*gotra-bhūmi*) clarifies the "innate seed" (*prakṛtistha-gotra*).
Subsequently, one enters the stage of the lineage of cultivated seeds (*bhāvanāgotra*).
Furthermore, there are two types of the nature-lineage (*prakṛtisthagotra*):
first, that which is with outflows (*sāsrava*), which, taking this as its cause, can produce the seven preparatory practices (*prayoga*) prior to the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).
Second, there are the untainted [seeds] capable of producing the untainted states from the stage of the Path of Seeing onward.
At the time of the acquired lineage (*śikṣita-gotra*), there are likewise two kinds:
first, those among the innate seeds (*prakṛti-gotra*) that are tainted; when these encounter conditions and are thus triggered, developed, and increased, they are then termed the acquired lineage.

From this point on, once the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) has arisen from the seeds of practice (*śikṣamāṇagotra*), the outflow-free (*anāsrava*) [dharmas] both perfuse the seeds and are themselves termed the seeds of practice.
Beiyun states:
"Because the naturally existing seeds (*dharmatā-bīja*) have not yet produced manifest results, they have not yet yielded their fruit."
There is no lengthening of the latencies through the perfuming of active manifestations,
because [the result] has not yet been accomplished through practice and arises from seeds of natural law (*dharmatā-bīja*); rather,
it is the active manifestation that subsequently perfumes.
This refers to the growth of the original seeds,
which is called the "fruition of cultivation.
The ancient masters of the *Dharmaparyāya* (Holding-the-Ground School) said:
The nature-seed (prakṛtisthagotra) is called subtle because it is the cause and effect of the dharma-body;
the practice-seed (samudānītagotra) is called coarse.
Regarding the fivefold Dharma-body (pañcāṅga-dharmakāya):
because it exists where it previously did not, a question is asked: [What is its cause?]
Regarding the question of whether such a lineage should be said to fall into a single continuum (*saṃtāna*) or many continua,
Jing states:
"The term 'continuum' refers to the body."
Does this śrāvaka lineage remain perpetually within the body of one and the same person from beginning to end,
or does it sometimes reside in this person's body and at other times in that person's body?
The meaning of the answer is that [the consciousness] constantly falls within the body of a single person from beginning to end;
this is explained below in the commentary.
First, the refutation by way of inversion.

Why is this so? If dharmas were of distinct characteristics yet existed simultaneously and evolved, even to the point of various modes of transmigration—this explains that the lineage (*gotra*) depends upon the fixed state of the physical basis (*āśraya*).
If that lineage and the physical basis were of distinct natures and operated simultaneously,
one could then say that it either depends on this body or depends on another body.
Since it has no separate entity, this seed of the body cannot fall into another body.
The following provides a sequential explanation:
"Such seeds do not possess distinct characteristics within the six sense bases," and so forth.
Since this seed does not possess a distinct characteristic separate from the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*),
the excellence of the six sense bases within the preceding and succeeding states of such a class of body is termed "possessing the lineage" (*gotra*).

Alternatively, one may directly consider that within the body of a single person, the eighteen *dhātus* themselves, in their preceding and succeeding moments of the same category, are termed a "continuum" (*saṃtāna*).

Now, the question is: does the spiritual lineage (*gotra*) share the same nature as True Suchness (*tathatā*) and thus pervade all eighteen *dhātus* across many continua, or does it fall within a single *dhātu* and a single continuum?
The answer states: "It falls solely within the single continuum of the *ālayavijñāna* and the mental realm (*manodhātu*).
As for the reason why it is said that it undergoes various forms of transmigration, this is permitted as a conventional designation."
If the eighteen elements (*dhātu*) possessed distinct natures and existed simultaneously at all times,
it might be granted that spiritual lineages (*gotra*) could fall into multiple continuities;
however, their presence and absence are currently not fixed.
Just as the five sense organs and five sense objects exist in the lower realms,
in the higher realms— namely, the heavens—
the five consciousnesses are entirely absent in the second dhyāna and above.
The sixth mental consciousness arises and ceases across various states;
it ceases within the two mindless attainments and in the heaven of non-conception.
In none of these is it the locus that serves as the support for the lineage (*gotra*).
Therefore, it is said that one perceives those various distinct continuities and various modes of transmigration.
Regarding the statement "such seeds... up to the excellence of the six sense bases":
if such seeds were to exist as a separate entity apart from the sixth consciousness, it would have to be admitted that they fall within multiple continuities.
However, this seed does not exist as a distinct characteristic separate from the six sense bases;
rather, it exists within the functional capacity of these seeds in the specific states of the categories of the ālayavijñāna and the manas.
It is said that this *manas-āyatana* is called "preeminent. T'ai states:
"The text of the author of the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, which establishes the seeds as having a distinct substance, is identical to this."
The ten material dharmas and the eight types of consciousness do not arise simultaneously as distinct entities in a continuous succession;
this is because the functional capacities of the ten material dharmas and the eight consciousnesses reside within the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) and lack individual, separate bodies.
They fall into a single continuum. Why?
Because when the ten material phenomena and the eight mental phenomena arise simultaneously, their respective entities, though distinct in character, exist together and function concurrently.
It is directly perceived that those various ten types of matter and eight types of mind each exist as distinct entities,
which flow in various ways through many kinds of continuities;
this is the meaning of a continuity consisting of multiple entities.
Now, from the perspective of the conforming gate (*anuvartana-mukha*), the untainted seeds do not possess a distinct characteristic separate from the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*).

Rather, it is upon this very same category of state within the six sense bases that there arises a superior capacity for producing the untainted; this is termed the "excellence of the six sense bases."
From beginningless time, that which can be apprehended as being one with the six sense bases and continuing in succession is termed "a single continuum" (*eka-santāna*).
This is explained in detail according to the Tripiṭaka;
its general meaning is the same as the interpretation of Jingchu.
Jizang further explains:
"The meaning herein consists of an initial interpretive explanation followed by the definitive explanation."
This refers to the various modes of transmigration of phenomena, even down to their most subtle forms; this is the explanation of the reversal [of that].

Herein, the intended meaning is that if seeds and the bases of the six sense-fields were distinct from one another, they could each have separate characteristics and proceed through various continuities and various modes of transmigration.
Just as with the ten bases of form and the six bases of consciousness,
so too these seeds do not possess distinct characteristics within the six bases; therefore,
one knows that they reside within a single continuum.
As explained in the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha-bhāṣya*:

with the exception of Central India, the remaining four Indias are also termed "border countries."
Furthermore, this region excludes those who are deluded and so forth; it is called *darśa*.
Those with skin diseases such as *ṣaḍala* are called *mleccha*.
Moreover, wherever the Three Jewels are present, that place is also termed the "Middle Country" (*madhyadeśa*).
If the Three Jewels are absent, all such places are called borderlands.

"Those who have attained the goal" (samyaktva-pratipanna) refers to those in the four fruits [of the śramaṇa]; they are called "noble ones" (ārya) and "virtuous persons" (satpuruṣa) because they have correctly attained the goal.
The *Nyāyānusāra* explains that the four paths and four fruits are termed "right practice" (*samyak-pratipatti*) and "right attainment" (*samyak-saṃprāpti*).
In the section analyzing the conditions for superiority and inferiority, the text is divided into four parts:
first, the question; second, the answer; third, the inquiry; and fourth, the explanation.
In the commentary,
first the [terms] are listed and then explained.
In the explanation, the two conditions are first explained individually.
The two conditions are explained in two ways;
the three factors are assigned in three ways.
First, regarding the initial [section]:
Jingyun said:
"I have heard the teaching on the method of entering the clear observation (*abhisamaya*) of the Four Noble Truths;
through internal right reflection, I shall immediately begin its cultivation."
From the five contemplations for settling the mind up to the supreme mundane dharma (*laukikāgradharma*),
these all serve as superior conditions in relation to the clear observation of the truths (*satyābhisamaya*).
If one has not yet given rise to the contemplative practices prior to the seven stages of expedient means (*saptavidha-upāya*),
these are termed inferior conditions.
If one enters the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) and proceeds from right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*) through to the full cultivation of all practices, [these are termed superior conditions].
Entering the realm of nirvana without remainder and so forth is called true cultivation. Tai says:
The wisdoms derived from hearing and reflection, and so forth, are called superior conditions;
all other external conditions are inferior conditions.
There are twelve types of inferior conditions.
This is the sequential explanation.
Within the section on "Perfection," it says: "First, cultivate the superior, pure faith."
This refers to the impure, pure faith that precedes the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).
Within the perfection of others,
"the long endurance of the Dharma teaching" means:
It is said: "Just as the lifespan of Śākyamuni Buddha was eighty years,
the World-Honored One Maitreya shall abide for sixty thousand years."
After Śākyamuni enters nirvāṇa, the True Dharma shall endure for five hundred years and the Semblance Dharma for one thousand years.
After Maitreya enters nirvāṇa, the Dharma shall likewise remain in the world for sixty thousand years.
Whether abiding or ceasing for such a duration, the True Dharma does not perish.

As for the statement, "One should know that this explains the principle by which that ultimate True Dharma abides and is realized," this refers to the fact that its realization and practice endure for a long time without perishing.
Regardless of the specific teaching,
it is therefore called the "ultimate true Dharma.
Thus, the *Abhidharmahṛdaya* states:
The Sūtras, Vinaya, and Abhidharma are called the conventional true Dharma;
the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment are said to be the ultimate truth.
Ji further stated:
This passage clarifies that during the five hundred years of the True Dharma (saddharma), there is realization through the True Dharma;
however, regarding the duration for which this Dharma remains, the textual sources differ.
According to the *Māyā-sūtra*, the True Dharma remains for five hundred years.

According to the *Mahākaruṇā-sūtra* and other authentic teachings, the True Dharma (*saddharma*) lasts for one thousand years, the Semblance Dharma (*pratirūpaka-dharma*) for another thousand years, and the Final Dharma (*paścima-dharma*) for ten thousand years.
Furthermore, the *Dharmasthiti-sūtra* by Nandimitra states regarding this Buddha-dharma:
After the kalpa of weapons, people grew weary of violence and all gave rise to a mind of compassion, ceasing to kill one another.
Treating each other with mutual pity as they would a father or a son,
their lifespans gradually increased until they reached a full hundred years.
The sixteen great Arhats, endowed with the three insights and six supernormal powers, and fully proficient in the eight liberations, the Tripitaka, and the twelve divisions of the scriptures,
have received the Buddha’s entrustment to uphold the True Dharma and benefit sentient beings, and thus do not enter parinirvāṇa.
Together with his remaining retinue of more than ten thousand great arhats, he caused the Tathāgata’s Tripiṭaka teachings to circulate in the world.
He transformed and guided sentient beings, constructing monasteries, ordaining monks, and practicing the precepts, meditative concentration, and wisdom; thus, the Buddha-dharma flourished.
When the human lifespan reaches its end at sixty thousand years and begins again at seventy thousand years,
all the Arhats will assemble and together construct a precious stūpa for all the relics of the Tathāgata.
The sixteen arhats, together with their retinues, circumambulated the stūpa to make offerings, scattering various fragrant flowers.
Having gazed upon it and paid their respects, they all ascended into the air and spoke these words:
Homage to the Blessed One, Śākyamuni Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha.
Having received his command, I shall protect and uphold the True Dharma and bring manifold benefits to gods and humans.
The Dharma-treasury has already exhausted its conditions and its cycle is complete;
now he takes his leave to enter parinirvāṇa.
Having spoken these words, he passed away.
All entered *nirvāṇa* without remainder simultaneously.
Their stūpas then sank into the earth until they reached the golden wheel at its base, where they came to rest.
The teachings of the Tripiṭaka had already vanished prior to the śarīras.
After one hundred years have passed,
this pure Dharma, along with the stūpas of the śarīras and all the arhats, will simultaneously vanish and perish.
At that time, the unsurpassed True Dharma of the World-Honored One Śākyamuni will be extinguished forever and no longer appear within this trichiliocosm.
Immediately following this, seventy billion pratyekabuddhas appeared simultaneously within this buddha-field.
When the lifespan of human beings reached eighty thousand years, the assembly of noble pratyekabuddhas all entered parinirvāṇa.
Afterwards, when Maitreya appears in the world, this will be sought;
at the end of the seventh fascicle of the *Baoshijing*, it largely accords with this record. As for those who exert themselves in the precepts, these are precisely the ten precepts of a śrāmaṇera.
It is also called *le-ce-jie* (śikṣāpada).

This is called "exertion" (pragraha) and also called "stopping evil.
As for "restraint of the sense faculties" (indriya-saṃvara):
This refers to the mindfulness and wisdom that guard the six sense faculties.
Regarding the statement, "knowing the measure in eating for the sake of ending [craving] and so forth," this shall be explained in the twenty-third fascicle.
Regarding the purification of the mind from factors conducive to hindrances:
one recognizes that from this mind arise factors conducive to greed, hatred, and so forth,
and immediately restrains and purifies them.
Regarding "dwelling with clear comprehension whether going or coming," and so forth,
this will be explained in detail in the twenty-fourth [chapter] on "Delighting in Seclusion."
Regarding the phrase "having correctly cultivated the stage of the beginner," Jing says: that is to say,
the previously mentioned states such as "abiding with correct knowledge" are designated as the stage of the beginner.
Master Ji said:
"This refers to the cultivation of the karma of the initial resolve for enlightenment, such as renouncing the household life and so forth.
Regarding 'extreme bedding,' the term 'extreme' (prānta) refers to the most inferior kind of bedding."
By means of such gradual cultivation, "even unto the immovable" refers to the subsequent inferior conditions;
"if he further attains that which relies upon the Four Noble Truths, even unto the attention induced by correct reasoning" refers to the preceding superior conditions.
Furthermore, that which is preceded by those [factors], beginning with right view and culminating in parinirvāṇa, is the true essence of cultivation.
Above, the essences of the three dharmas were cited;
below, their respective designations are assigned.
Regarding the statement in the third section, "The craving for the ālayavijñāna binds one in all its modes," Jing says:
"One reckons the ālaya as the self."
Because of this attachment to the self and attachment to the requisites of the self, the ālayavijñāna is bound in all its modes.
Furthermore, due to this attachment, other afflictions arise and grow within the ālayavijñāna.
Therefore, it is said that by being attached to and dependent upon [the self], they become immeasurable dharmas.
Since there is no path of abandonment, they are difficult to uproot;

Because they cannot provide rescue, all unwholesome dharmas remain ultimately firm and persist for a long duration. This concludes the detailed exposition according to the interpretation of the Tripiṭaka.
It is defiled and concealed;

Tai [Xuanzang] says:

The name *ālaya* means "storehouse" (*kośa*) and "concealment" (*gupti*),
because one is attached to and conceals the various requisites of life;
it is like the water-born, foul-smelling snail that makes a conch-like sound and moves like a dog.
Jingyun: When a snail moves through water, it causes the water to become turbid and foul,
just like the saliva of a cow.
In the western regions there is the "conch-sound" (śaṅkha-nāda).
There are dogs that bark like that conch-sound and move with the gait of a dog;
this is a metaphor for those bhikṣus who harbor greed and other afflictions within.
Tài further explained:
"The Buddha-dharma is like water;
a bhikṣu who breaks the precepts is like a snail amidst a multitude of impurities in the water."
Furthermore, just as a dog may have a voice like a conch shell yet possesses the behavior of a dog,
so too is a bhikṣu who violates the precepts: his outward form resembles that of a true practitioner, but he is not in reality.
The actual nature of unwholesome conduct.
Explanation.
The text of the fourth section is divided into two parts.
The question comes first and the answer follows.
Within the answer there are three parts;
first, twenty-three individuals are enumerated.
Next, the text cites and explains [the passage].
Finally, it concludes by describing the manifestation of Buddhahood.
If there is no leisure within saṃsāra...
"Those born in difficult places" means,
according to the Sanskrit original,
"those born in states lacking leisure."
This is called being in a state where there is no leisure to enter the Path.
It is like the worldly expression, "there is no leisure to do this matter.
Regarding the distant [obstacles], there are two types.
First, due to the remoteness of time:
although this person possesses the spiritual lineage,
they must pass through many hundreds of thousands of births.
Now, encountering superior conditions, one develops the resolve and attains excellence.
Regarding those whose application is distant:
such persons abide solely within the spiritual lineage (*gotra*).
Yet they have not yet entered [the path] and are unable to quickly encounter superior conditions to give rise to superior application;
however, after three more births, they will be able to give rise to application and attain entry into nirvāṇa.
Regarding those who attain parinirvāṇa after a long duration, it requires passing through many lifetimes. Within the category of those who attain it after a short duration, there are two types:
first, those for whom the time is near; [second, those for whom the time is distant].
This person has already practiced through many lifetimes;
they dwell in their final birth, their final existence, and their final body,
and by means of this very body, they shall attain nirvāṇa.
Birth-existence (*upapatti-bhava*) and the physical body (*śarīra*) are identical in meaning though different in expression.
When contrasted with those who undergo seven births or fourteen births,
this person abides in their final birth.
Regarding the state of continuity within the twenty-five existences of the three realms of existence,
this person abides in the final existence;
"existence" (bhava) carries the sense of being a basis and the sense of an accumulation.
From time immemorial, bodies have been linked in succession;
for this person who has attained the Way, all subsequent births are extinguished,
and abiding in his final body, he shall enter parinirvāṇa.
"Or that which is to be realized immediately after this very moment" refers to abiding in the vajra-mind (*vajracitta*).
"Proximate through application" (*prayoga*) means...
Either in this very life they will soon be able to initiate application,
or after passing through one more birth they will be able to initiate application,
or they will attain nirvana before long through such application.
All are termed "proximate through application.
Regarding the stage of entry (the sixth part, upper section), within the stage of entry,

Next, the explanation proceeds according to the gates,
followed by a general summary.
Within the explanation of the first gate:
This refers to a person (*pudgala*) who abides in the lineage (*gotra*) and has naturally perfected the seeds of *nirvāṇa*;
it restates that the aforementioned "ground of the lineage" (*gotrabhūmi*) is precisely the "nature-lineage" (*prakṛtistha-gotra*).
If, at that time, a Buddha appears in the world and one is born in a central land and so forth— as described below—
this very emergence and entry into the essence of the stages (*bhūmi*) constitutes the lineage of cultivation (*śikṣāgotra*).
Within this, there are two types:
first, those with outflows (sāsrava) that can produce the seven preparatory practices prior to the path of seeing;
second, those without outflows (anāsrava) that can produce all uncontaminated practices from the path of seeing onward.

Now, the statement that "a Buddha has appeared in the world" and so forth, up to "hearing the Dharma from him," refers to the conditions for the emergence and entry into the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
The attainment of initial right faith (*samyak-prasāda*) and so forth constitutes the essence (*ātman*) of this emergence and entry.

From this point onward, that which serves as the basis for long-term faith and so forth by means of this "acceptance of the Dharma" (dharmānudharma) is precisely what was previously termed right faith, ethical discipline, learning, wisdom, and relinquishment; these are called the acceptance of the Dharma.
To accept and practice faith and so forth for the sake of the dharma of nirvāṇa is called "receiving the dharma" (*dharmaparigraha*).
By means of that reception of the dharma as a cause, one obtains a superior body in the subsequent birth, which serves as the basis for even more excellent faith and so forth.
Furthermore, by means of increasingly superior dharmas such as faith, up to that which is the path, the way, or the right track for attaining nirvāṇa and proceeding toward nirvāṇa—
the "path" here refers to the seven paths of expedient means.
The "path" refers to the factors of enlightenment, the eightfold noble path, and so forth;
the "tracks" refer to the contemplation of the four noble truths.
Thus, when the sages of old traveled upon the aforementioned path and trod upon the aforementioned tracks, they were able to attain *nirvāṇa* and proceed toward *nirvāṇa*.
At that time, he is able to draw forth the path of skillful means,
enter the Eightfold Noble Path,
and tread upon the tracks of the Four Noble Truths.
One is able to progress gradually until reaching the ultimate.
Regarding this, Master Bei explains:
"It requires waiting upon a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) to plant the roots of merit conducive to liberation (mokṣabhāgīya)."
Now, the Buddha and his disciples are called "good friends" (*kalyāṇamitra*).
Furthermore, according to the *Śīla-saṃvara-sūtra*, by encountering the Buddha and the Akaniṣṭha devas, one plants the seeds for the stage of excellence and liberation (*viśeṣa-vimukti-bhāga*).
This refers to the Bodhisattva of the tenth stage, as it is the locus for the gathering of karmic retribution.
Master Tai further stated:
"Attaining a superior body that accords with the Path is called 'the excellence of the various faculties.'"
The second is the door of formal establishment.
First the question is posed,
then the answer is given.
The conclusion follows later.
In the response, eight phrases are first listed,
which are subsequently explained in sequence.
The explanation consists of three parts:
first, the interpretation of the eight gates;
second, the subsumption of the eight into six layers to further explain their accomplishment.
Regarding the subsequent explanation of the speed of entry,
the eight stages are subsumed into six.
First, the six positions in which these individuals are subsumed are restated.
Next, the six stages are examined and explained.
The subsequent exposition of the six stages arises from the preceding and leads into the succeeding.
As for the six stages:
First, those who abide in the spiritual lineage but have not yet entered [the path].
Second, those who have accomplished inferior roots of virtue and, although they have already set out, have not yet practiced through successive births.
Third, those with middling roots of virtue who have already practiced through successive births but have not yet reached the final body that enters the state of an ārya.
Fourth, those with superior roots of goodness abide in that final stage of cultivation and enter the body of a noble one (*ārya*).
Fifth, those with ultimate skillful means proceed from the first fruit to further sever and cultivate what has not yet been attained, until they reach arhatship.
The sixth is one who has reached the ultimate, namely the Arhat.
Regarding this, the *Bèiyún* (Complete Explanation) states:

"The preceding eight persons do not exhaustively encompass all individuals, as they are only included within the two categories of those in the stage of application (*prayoga*) and those on the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*)."
Although this interpretation exists, it does not accord with the text;
for in the third vehicle, the preceding arises before the subsequent,
and herein the former is first distinguished and then the latter.
The subsequent section clarifies that this encompasses all śrāvakas.
Within the third part, which explains the distinctions in the speed of cultivation,
there are three general categories.

First, those for whom it is extremely long: these śrāvakas require at least sixty kalpas to cultivate the roots of merit conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya-kuśalamūla*) before attaining parinirvāṇa in their final body.
Second, those for whom it is not extremely long: there are those who attain parinirvāṇa after many lifetimes, or even as few as one kalpa.
Regarding those who attain parinirvāṇa with the utmost swiftness, they must pass through three lifetimes.
In the first lifetime, they resolve their minds and cultivate the wholesome dharmas conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*),
namely, the five contemplations for settling the mind (*pañcākārāḥ śamathāḥ*) and the general and specific applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*).

In the second birth, one again cultivates the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*); from the general foundations of mindfulness, one cultivates and proceeds toward the stages of Heat (*uṣmagata*) and Summits (*mūrdhan*).
Alternatively, entering into Lower Patience (*adhimātra-kṣānti*) or Middle Patience (*madhyama-kṣānti*) is termed "attainment."
In the third birth, one again arises from either the lower or middle degree of patience (*kṣānti*) into the higher patience (*adhimātra-kṣānti*) and the supreme mundane dharma (*laukikāgra-dharma*),
